# upigz

> A fast parallel gzip/DEFLATE decoder in Rust, built for the single-member file.

upigz is a parallel gzip/DEFLATE decoder in Rust, built for large single-member files: it
decodes chunks speculatively, before their 32 KiB history is known, then resolves them. It is
a research prototype. Each link below is the Markdown version of a page of
https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/.

# Start here

# upigz

μpigz decodes gzip in parallel, including the case other parallel decoders find hardest: one large member, such as the Wikidata JSON dump's single 157 GB member. It splits the member into chunks, decodes each one before it knows the 32 KiB of history its matches may reach back into, and then fixes up what it couldn't know.

- **A finder** scans each chunk for a plausible dynamic-block header.
- **Pass 1** decodes each chunk into 16-bit symbols, where an unknown history byte is a marker.
- **The windows** are handed on in order, each chunk's last 32 KiB resolved through the previous chunk's.
- **Resolution and the CRC** run in parallel; the CRC-32 and ISIZE are checked against the trailer.

A chunk start is used only if the previous chunk's decode lands on it exactly, so a wrong guess by the finder can cost time but never correctness.

On a 4-core research host it decodes a 1.34 GB single-member Wikidata file at 1.21 GB/s end to end, against rapidgzip's 0.80 on the same cores: [the benchmarks](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/benchmarks/index.md>) have the figures and their caveats. They are indicative only. A 10-core workstation decides the ranking.

upigz is a research prototype: see [getting started](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/getting-started/index.md>) for building it and what it doesn't do yet.

## Where to go

- [Getting started](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/getting-started/index.md>): building upigz and running its parallel `zcat`.
- [Benchmarks](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/benchmarks/index.md>): the research host's figures, single thread and parallel.
- [Journals](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/index.md>): the research record, entry by entry.
- [Blog](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/blog/index.md>): what the experiments find, as they find it.
- The source is on [GitHub](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz>).

# Getting started

upigz is a research prototype: it is not on crates.io, and its command line will change.

## Build

You need Rust (the version is pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml`, so `rustup` fetches it) and ISA-L's development files, for the `isal` comparison arm (`libisal-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu). The build targets `x86-64-v3`, that is AVX2 and BMI2 (`.cargo/config.toml`).

```sh
git clone https://github.com/lmmx/upigz
cd upigz
cargo build --release
```

## Decode a file

```sh
target/release/upigz zcat file.gz 4 1024 > file
```

The arguments are the file, the thread count and the chunk size in KiB. An optional fourth caps how many chunks are in flight at once (by default, threads + 2). The output goes to stdout, and the CRC-32 and ISIZE are checked against the trailer: a mismatch aborts. `UPIGZ_STATS=1` prints the number of chunks and the finder's time to stderr.

## Check the speculative decode

```sh
target/release/upigz spectest 50
```

This builds 50 random DEFLATE streams and checks, at every block start, that decoding without the history and then filling it in gives exactly the sequential decoder's output. CI runs it on every push.

## Not yet

- Files with more than one gzip member (the Wikidata dump starts with a 22-byte one).
- Recovering when the finder's guess is wrong: today it stops with an error.
- Chunks shorter than a 32 KiB window.
- The same errors as zlib on corrupt input.
- Fuzzing.

# Benchmarks

# Benchmarks

Every figure on this page comes from the research host, a shared 4-vCPU cloud VM (a Sapphire Rapids-class Xeon at 2.1 GHz, 4 real cores, no hardware PMU), and is copied unchanged from the journals. **They are indicative only.** The i9-10900K workstation, with 10 cores and 20 threads, decides the real ranking, through registered recipes that don't exist yet.

How the figures are made:

- **Paired rounds.** Every arm runs from one harness binary, once a round in shuffled order; the first round is dropped.
- **Ratios** are the geometric mean of per-round time ratios, with a 95% t interval on the log scale (`scripts/ratio.py`). Below 1 is faster. An A/A duplicate arm lands within about ±4%, so the harness resolves differences of about 5%.
- **Correctness first.** Every arm is checked byte-exact against the reference before timing.
- **The build** targets `x86-64-v3` (AVX2 and BMI2, the i9's instruction set; no AVX-512).

The corpora are 64 MiB each of real Wikidata JSON (the head of `latest-all.json.gz`), source code and binaries, as a single member at `gzip -6` and `-9`, as 1 MiB members (`m1M`) and as BGZF, and a 1.34 GB single-member Wikidata file for the parallel runs.

## Parallel, end to end

On the 1.34 GB single-member Wikidata file (the real dump's head, recompressed with `gzip -6`): page-cache read, decode, CRC-32 and ISIZE checked, bytes to /dev/null. From [the second entry](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/kernel-and-parallel/index.md>).

|  | GB/s | time vs rapidgzip -P4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **upigz -P4, 1 MiB chunks (unchecked build)** | **1.21** | **0.677 \[0.616, 0.744\]** |
| **upigz -P4, 1 MiB chunks (safe build)** | **1.15** | **0.750 \[0.698, 0.807\]** (separate race) |
| upigz -P3 | 0.94 | 0.864 \[0.810, 0.921\] |
| rapidgzip 0.16.2 -P4 (default / `--verify`) | 0.80 / 0.82 | 1.000 / 0.980 |
| igzip (ISA-L 2.31), 1 thread | 0.81 | 1.003 |

The same race as a chart, generated from `runs/race-big4.txt` by `docs/scripts/figures.py` (the numbers are in [`results.json`](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/assets/data/results.json>)). Six paired rounds; the time ratio is the geometric mean of per-round ratios, with a 95% interval.

rapidgzip scales poorly on this host (its P2 is slower than its sequential P1 path), so the i9's 10 cores decide the real ranking.

How the parallel decoder got there, upigz -P4 against rapidgzip -P4:

| time vs rapidgzip -P4 | version |
| --- | --- |
| 1.591 \[1.194, 2.119\] | 1\. all chunks alive at once |
| 0.849 \[0.793, 0.909\] | 2\. **bounded** |
| 1.130 \[1.029, 1.241\] | 3\. resolution as a queued task |
| **0.677** \[0.616, 0.744\] | 4\. **window hand-off off the chain** |

1. Every chunk's buffers were alive at once, and decode, then CRC, then write ran one after another. In memory, with warm buffers, it reached 1.69 GB/s.
2. At most threads + 2 chunks in flight, recycled buffers, streamed output.
3. A regression: it exposed a serial chain.
4. The next window is derived before a chunk is queued, with separate cursors for windows and writes.

## Single thread, in memory

Time vs libdeflate 1.26.1, in the same binary. The upigz rows are from [the kernel's parity entry](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-11-22-kernel-parity.md>) (`runs/k1-*.txt`, 11 rounds), after \#16. The ISA-L and zlib-rs rows are from the first race ([the second entry](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/kernel-and-parallel/index.md>), `runs/sota-*.txt`). Each is a ratio against libdeflate measured in its own binary, so they compare across the two runs.

|  | Wikidata -6 | source -6 | binary -6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **upigz kernel, unchecked build** | **1.000** \[0.986, 1.014\] | **0.997** \[0.961, 1.034\] | **1.030** \[0.984, 1.078\] |
| upigz kernel, safe build (the default) | 1.102 \[1.086, 1.119\] | 1.162 \[1.112, 1.214\] | 1.179 \[1.096, 1.267\] |
| ISA-L 2.31 | 1.172 | 1.138 | 1.149 |
| zlib-rs 0.6.8 | 1.366 | 1.410 | 1.391 |

The single-thread table as a chart, generated from `runs/k1-*.txt` and `runs/sota-*.txt` by `docs/scripts/figures.py`. The dashed line is libdeflate; whiskers are 95% intervals. The unchecked kernel is level with libdeflate, not ahead of it.

What moved the kernel, step by step (unchecked-build time vs libdeflate, on Wikidata / source / binary):

| step | ratios |
| --- | --- |
| v1: entry-driven consume, preload, 3 literals per refill, margins, word copies | 1.28 / 1.17 / 1.23 |
| unconditional first copy chunk (two 16-byte chunks, then libdeflate's 5×8) | no change |
| `bzhi`/`shrx` field extraction without masks, subtract the whole entry | no change |
| **libdeflate's literal→match fallthrough** (no refill on the transition) | **1.21 / 1.13 / 1.15** |
| **table build: libdeflate's doubling method for complete codes** | **1.07 / 1.09 / 1.09** |
| generic (inlined) entry constructors, 4 precode symbols per refill | 1.06 / 1.08 / 1.14 (noisy run) |
| **one `bzhi` for the extra bits** (\#16; the host restarted, so a fresh baseline: 1.079 / 1.098 / 1.113) | **1.000 / 0.997 / 1.030** |

## What the i9 run will decide

Everything above is from a 4-vCPU VM, where rapidgzip scales poorly. The i9-10900K workstation (10 cores, 20 threads, dual-channel DDR4) decides, through a recipe whose decision rule is registered before its data. The first recipe races upigz against rapidgzip at the same thread counts, and against igzip, on the single-member Wikidata file. It will settle two questions:

- **Does the lead hold with more cores?** On the VM upigz -P4 took 0.677× rapidgzip -P4's time. At 8 and 10 threads both decoders are expected to approach the memory bandwidth limit, and rapidgzip's design writes and rereads 16-bit symbols for every output byte.
- **Where does upigz's own scaling stop?** The thread sweep shows the knee, and with it whether the next lever is the 16-bit pass-1 kernel or memory traffic: the re-decode bet in the [research charter's frontier](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/blob/master/docs/team/research-charter/FRONTIER.md>).

The recipe is registered, with its rule, in [the i9 race's registration](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-11-22-i9-race-registration.md>): `just submit bench-i9-race`, judged by `bench/i9_race.py`. It is VALID PASS if the 95% interval of time(upigz-P10) / time(rapidgzip-P10) lies wholly below 1.00, with an A/A control inside \[0.95, 1.05\]. It is queued for the workstation, and its result will be posted here.

## Interleaving within a thread (closed)

Decoding K independent members round-robin in one thread, as time vs `ours-k1` (below 1 is faster). It doesn't pay on real data. From [the first entry](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/interleaved-inflate/index.md>).

| file | k2 | k4 | A/A |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wikidata m1M (first run, rolled loop) | 1.245 \[1.188, 1.305\] | 1.177 \[1.128, 1.228\] | 1.018 \[0.949, 1.092\] |
| wikidata m1M (unrolled) | 1.038 \[0.996, 1.081\] | 1.108 \[1.043, 1.178\] | 1.027 \[0.980, 1.077\] |
| wikidata BGZF | 1.023 \[0.924, 1.133\] | 1.084 \[1.021, 1.151\] | 0.966 \[0.900, 1.036\] |
| source m1M | 0.982 \[0.914, 1.054\] | 1.100 \[1.006, 1.204\] | 0.967 \[0.933, 1.002\] |
| source BGZF | 0.998 \[0.955, 1.042\] | 1.102 \[1.046, 1.162\] | 1.018 \[0.956, 1.083\] |
| binary m1M | 1.035 \[0.980, 1.093\] | 1.042 \[0.989, 1.098\] | 0.973 \[0.900, 1.052\] |
| binary BGZF | 1.073 \[1.010, 1.140\] | 1.129 \[1.066, 1.194\] | 1.023 \[0.963, 1.088\] |

On symbol-dense controls the mechanism exists:

| Wikidata m1M re-encoded | k2 | k3 | k4 | k8 | libdeflate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY` | 0.781 \[0.734, 0.831\] | 0.798 | **0.775** \[0.716, 0.839\] | 0.886 | 0.599 |
| `Z_RLE` (also \~all literals) | **0.737** \[0.691, 0.785\] | 0.778 | 0.784 | — | 0.624 |

Real gzip data is match-dominated, which is why:

|  | symbols/byte | literal share of symbols | bytes from matches | mean match len | dist \<8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wikidata | **0.121** | 0.695 | 91.6% | 24.7 | 1.4% |
| source | 0.237 | 0.623 | 85.3% | 9.6 | 3.2% |
| binary | 0.249 | 0.642 | 84.0% | 9.4 | 3.0% |

# History

How upigz's decoding speed, CPU time and peak memory have changed on master, measured on GitHub's runners by the CI benchmark (`.github/workflows/bench.yml`, [`bench/ci_bench.py`](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/blob/master/bench/ci_bench.py>)). The machinery, the records' layout and these charts are lmmx/mibz2's.

- **The workload.** One gzip member: the first 256 MiB of the dated Wikidata JSON dump of 16 November 2026, whole lines, compressed with `gzip -6 -n` (40 MB). Every arm's output is checked against its SHA-256 before any timing.
- **The runs.** Each push to master that touches the decoder decodes it whole with that commit's `upigz zcat` at 1, 2 and 4 threads, beside the other decoders ([Alternatives](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/benchmarks/alternatives/index.md>)), for 10 shuffled rounds on one runner. At 1 thread upigz runs its byte kernel, with no speculation.
- **One runner CPU model at a time.** GitHub's runners vary in CPU model. A line joins only records from the same model, and the chart shows the model with the most records by default. These figures are a trend, not a ranking: a ranking is decided on the i9-10900K ([the research charter](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/blob/master/docs/team/research-charter/README.md>)).
- **A line never joins** another bench meaning (a version that redefined the figures; [the benchmark's changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/blob/master/bench/CHANGELOG.md>)) or another content of a corpus.
- **Merge by merge, chained** (the chart at the top). Each pull request's benchmark runs its head against its base on one runner, both builds, for 10 rounds in a shuffled order. Each merge keeps that paired change ([`bench/links.py`](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/blob/master/bench/links.py>)), and the chart multiplies the changes. The band is the product's 95% interval. Merges from before pull requests were benchmarked are backfilled: the merge against its first parent, run the same way. A merge that left the decoder alone is an A/A pair, drawn hollow, and adds nothing.
- **Absolute figures** (the charts below it) are master's records: each merge's upigz in MB/s, CPU seconds and peak RSS, on whichever runner the run drew. The backfilled merges share one runner, so they are directly comparable.

Loading the benchmark history…

The raw records are on the [`bench-results`](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/tree/bench-results>) branch: `records.jsonl`, a line a recorded commit; `runs/<commit>.json`, its figures; `raw/<commit>.jsonl`, every timed run.

A ratio above 1× is the alternative taking longer (or more memory) than upigz at the same thread count.

| decoder | what runs | threads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rapidgzip | 0.16.2, from PyPI: `rapidgzip -P T --verify -dc` | chunk-parallel |
| igzip | ISA-L 2.31's command-line tool: `igzip -dc` | single-threaded |
| libdeflate | `libdeflate-gunzip -c` (Ubuntu's libdeflate-tools) | single-threaded |
| pigz | `pigz -dc` (its decode is one thread, with reading, writing and the check in others) | single-threaded |
| gzip | GNU gzip: `gzip -dc` | single-threaded |

**Single-threaded decoders run at 1 thread only.** At 2 and 4 threads only upigz and rapidgzip run.

**These are a runner's figures, not a ranking.** The research host's and the i9's figures are on the [Benchmarks](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/benchmarks/index.md>) page; a ranking is decided on the i9-10900K.

The latest record: [`7e092a6`](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/commit/7e092a6ea42377f0f127aa970f9f35c1b10dabfc>) (2026-11-22).

**bench 1.0.0**, 10 rounds, on AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (4 cores) · [run](<https://github.com/lmmx/upigz/actions/runs/45063025782>). Each arm decodes the whole file end to end (CRC checked), output to /dev/null; ratios are each arm's time over upigz's at the same thread count, paired by round, with a 95% interval (below 1 is faster than upigz).

Versions: rustc 1.99.1, rapidgzip 0.16.2, igzip 2.31.1, libdeflate 1.23, pigz 2.8, gzip 1.14.

# Journals

# Journals

Each entry is a dated record of one question: what was asked, the rule fixed before the data, the setup, the results and what comes next. The sources are `docs/journal/` in the repository, and the raw rounds are in `runs/`. Every figure is from the research host, a shared 4-vCPU cloud VM, and is indicative only.

- [Does mibz2's interleaving idea work for gzip?](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/interleaved-inflate/index.md>): no, not within a thread; the parallelism that pays is across cores.
- [The single-thread kernel and the first parallel win](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/kernel-and-parallel/index.md>): the kernel within 4–12% of libdeflate, and a streaming parallel decoder ahead of rapidgzip on 4 cores.
- [Speculative decode: the theorem, checked before any proof](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/speculative-theorem/index.md>): the statement, a counterexample hunt that found none, and a plan for a Lean proof.

# Does mibz2's interleaving idea work for gzip? (2026-11-22)

**Verdict: no, not within a thread.** On real data, decoding K independent DEFLATE members round-robin in one thread is never faster than decoding them one after another. It is often slower: K=2 takes 0.98–1.09× and K=4 1.04–1.16× the sequential time, across three corpora and two member layouts. The mechanism exists: on symbol-dense streams (one literal per byte), interleaving makes decoding about 1.28× faster. But real gzip data is match-dominated (0.12–0.25 symbols per output byte), so the serial bit-position chain that interleaving hides is only about a third of the decode time.

The parallelism that pays is across cores. On independent members, libdeflate gets 2.1 GB/s from 2 threads and 3.2 GB/s from 3, against 1.16 GB/s on one. Per the brief's rule ("only if step 2 wins"), the speculative single-member step was not started.

Host: a shared 4-vCPU cloud VM (Intel Xeon @ 2.1 GHz, model not exposed). It has no hardware PMU: `perf_event_open` returns ENOENT for every hardware event, so the mechanism below is inferred from controlled variants and generated code, not from counters. Timings are indicative. The ratios are paired, but the absolute GB/s will move on the i9.

## Question and the rule fixed before the data

Louis asked whether mibz2's first idea, interleaved chains for memory-level parallelism, works for gzip. In mibz2, the interleaved inverse-BWT walks hide DRAM latency. In inflate, the serial chain is the bit position (each code's start depends on the previous code's length), and window copies mostly hit L1/L2. So interleaving could only hide *decode* latency, via instruction-level parallelism across streams.

The rule, from the brief: run the speculative single-member work only if K-way interleaving in one thread beats sequential decoding of the same K members. Ratios are reported with 95% intervals over paired, shuffled-order rounds. It was stated in the brief rather than frozen in a registration file, which this scratch setup doesn't have yet.

## Setup

- **Probe decoder** (`src/inflate.rs`): a minimal safe-Rust inflate.
- 11-bit litlen and 8-bit distance tables with subtables.
- Lengths and distances precombined with their extra bits.
- libdeflate's branch-free 8-byte refill (≥56 bits per symbol, one refill per symbol).
- 8-byte word copies when distance ≥8; fill when distance =1; byte loop otherwise.
- The hot loop is `hotN::<B>`: N streams advanced round-robin, B symbols at a time. It is unrolled by macro with literal indices, so each stream's state is a scalar. **K=1 is the same code**, so `ours-k1` vs `ours-kN` isolates interleaving.
- **Baselines, in memory, raw DEFLATE body into a preallocated buffer, no CRC:** libdeflate 1.26.1 (`libdeflater`), zlib-ng (`libz-ng-sys` 1.1.33), zlib-rs 0.6.8 (`libz-rs-sys`) and miniz\_oxide 0.9.1.
- **Correctness:** every arm on every file is checked byte-exact against the original before timing, with output buffers poisoned between arms. Each of our members must end exactly at its trailer.
- **Corpus**, 64 MiB of each:
- real Wikidata JSON, the head of `latest-all.json.gz`;
- source code (Python stdlib plus `/usr/include` as a tar);
- binaries (`/usr/bin` plus shared libraries as a tar).

Each comes as a single member at gzip -6 and -9, as 1 MiB members (level 6, 64 per file), and as BGZF (65 280 raw bytes per member, about 1 029 members). Literal-only controls use zlib's `Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY` and `Z_RLE` strategies.

- **Harness** (`src/main.rs`): one binary, pinned to one core (`taskset -c 2`). Each round runs every arm once in shuffled order; round 0 is dropped. The ratio is the geometric mean of per-round time ratios, with a t interval on the log scale (`scripts/ratio.py`). `ours-k1-aa` is an A/A duplicate: it lands within ±4% of 1.0 everywhere, so the harness resolves differences of about 5%.

Found on the way: **the real `latest-all.json.gz` is a 22-byte member holding `[\n`, followed by one 157 GB member.** The target case is single-member, so independent members can't come for free.

## Results

### 1\. Interleaving on real data (time vs `ours-k1`; below 1 = faster)

| file | k2 | k4 | A/A |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wikidata m1M (first run, rolled loop) | 1.245 \[1.188, 1.305\] | 1.177 \[1.128, 1.228\] | 1.018 \[0.949, 1.092\] |
| wikidata m1M (unrolled) | 1.038 \[0.996, 1.081\] | 1.108 \[1.043, 1.178\] | 1.027 \[0.980, 1.077\] |
| wikidata BGZF | 1.023 \[0.924, 1.133\] | 1.084 \[1.021, 1.151\] | 0.966 \[0.900, 1.036\] |
| source m1M | 0.982 \[0.914, 1.054\] | 1.100 \[1.006, 1.204\] | 0.967 \[0.933, 1.002\] |
| source BGZF | 0.998 \[0.955, 1.042\] | 1.102 \[1.046, 1.162\] | 1.018 \[0.956, 1.083\] |
| binary m1M | 1.035 \[0.980, 1.093\] | 1.042 \[0.989, 1.098\] | 0.973 \[0.900, 1.052\] |
| binary BGZF | 1.073 \[1.010, 1.140\] | 1.129 \[1.066, 1.194\] | 1.023 \[0.963, 1.088\] |

The rows from wikidata BGZF down come from the grid rounds (`runs/grid-*`), with 9 paired rounds each.

K=6 and K=8 get steadily worse: 1.19 and 1.29 on Wikidata m1M. Batching (B=4 symbols per stream per turn) is no better than B=1.

**The first run was invalid as a test, and why matters.** LLVM did not unroll the runtime `for i in 0..N` loop, so each stream's bit buffer lived in a stack array indexed at run time. That put a store-and-reload on every symbol, directly on the serial chain. `hot::<8,1>` was 624 instructions, about one copy of the step. Unrolling by macro (a 295-instruction body per stream) took K=2 from 1.245 to 1.038. The rolled form is kept as the `-r` arm: K=4 rolled costs 1.180. Lesson: **interleaving in Rust has to be unrolled by hand.** Check the disassembly, not the source.

### 2\. Symbol-dense controls: the mechanism exists

| Wikidata m1M re-encoded | k2 | k3 | k4 | k8 | libdeflate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY` | 0.781 \[0.734, 0.831\] | 0.798 | **0.775** \[0.716, 0.839\] | 0.886 | 0.599 |
| `Z_RLE` (also \~all literals) | **0.737** \[0.691, 0.785\] | 0.778 | 0.784 | — | 0.624 |

With one predictable literal per byte, `ours-k1` runs at about 9 cycles per symbol at the 2.1 GHz nominal clock, the latency of refill → lookup → shift. Interleaving 2–4 streams brings that to about 7, which is likely the instruction-throughput bound of this kernel, since each literal carries bounds checks. Past K=4, register pressure wins and the gain fades.

**libdeflate on one stream (0.60×) still beats our best interleave.** Its literal path (several literals per refill, entries pre-shifted for the `bitsleft -= entry` trick) shortens the chain more than interleaving hides it.

### 3\. Why real data doesn't benefit: the symbol census (`--features census`)

|  | symbols/byte | literal share of symbols | bytes from matches | mean match len | dist \<8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wikidata | **0.121** | 0.695 | 91.6% | 24.7 | 1.4% |
| source | 0.237 | 0.623 | 85.3% | 9.6 | 3.2% |
| binary | 0.249 | 0.642 | 84.0% | 9.4 | 3.0% |

At about 9 cycles per symbol, the chain costs Wikidata roughly 1.1 of its 3.0 cycles per byte (36%), and source or binary roughly 2.1 of 5.3 (40%). The rest is match copying and its data-dependent branches: the literal-vs-match branch, copy loops with variable trip counts, and the short-distance paths. Within one stream, the out-of-order core already overlaps those copies with the next symbol's decode, because a copy feeds nothing on the bit chain.

So the most interleaving could hide is the 36–40% that is chain latency. In practice it hides none of it, because the extra streams compete for the same load/store and branch resources and every mispredict flushes all of them. This is inference: no PMU here, so the branch-mispredict and port-pressure split should be confirmed on the i9 with `perf stat -e branch-misses,cycles,uops_dispatched.port_*`.

### 4\. State of the art, single thread

In memory (raw DEFLATE, time vs libdeflate; GB/s for libdeflate):

| file | libdeflate GB/s | zlib-rs | zlib-ng | ours-k1 | miniz\_oxide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wikidata -6 | 1.131 | 1.35 | 1.43 | 1.81 | 1.86 |
| wikidata -9 | 1.174 | 1.40 | 1.47 | 1.86 | 1.89 |
| wikidata m1M | 1.210 | 1.33 | 1.46 | 1.75 | 1.88 |
| wikidata BGZF | 1.053 | 1.38 | 1.43 | 1.79 | 1.98 |
| source -6 | 0.686 | 1.36 | 1.52 | 1.74 | 2.02 |
| source -9 | 0.683 | 1.36 | 1.57 | 1.76 | 2.09 |
| source m1M | 0.692 | 1.32 | 1.47 | 1.72 | 2.00 |
| source BGZF | 0.632 | 1.34 | 1.45 | 1.64 | 1.89 |
| binary -6 | 0.574 | 1.37 | 1.49 | 1.67 | 2.02 |
| binary -9 | 0.574 | 1.39 | 1.48 | 1.72 | 1.93 |
| binary m1M | 0.583 | 1.33 | 1.40 | 1.62 | 1.96 |
| binary BGZF | 0.553 | 1.37 | 1.45 | 1.61 | 1.97 |

CLI, end to end (page-cache read, inflate, CRC, write to /dev/null), GB/s, 8 paired rounds (`scripts/cli_ab.py`):

| file | igzip (ISA-L 2.31) | libdeflate-gunzip | rapidgzip -P1 | rapidgzip -P4 | pigz | gzip |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wikidata -6 | **0.821** | 0.671 | 0.497 | 0.540 | 0.346 | 0.198 |
| source -6 | 0.539 | 0.469 | 0.387 | **0.590** | 0.209 | 0.137 |
| binary -6 | 0.469 | 0.416 | 0.353 | **0.488** | 0.186 | 0.128 |
| wikidata BGZF | 0.856 | **1.060** | 0.513 | 0.883 | 0.324 | 0.198 |
| wikidata m1M | 1.041 | **1.143** | 0.552 | 1.034 | 0.375 | 0.206 |

Two things in this table are effects of how the tools handle memory, not of their decoders:

- **libdeflate-gunzip runs at 0.67 GB/s on the single-member file but 1.14 on the same bytes in 1 MiB members.** In memory, with a reused buffer, it is 1.13 on the single member. The difference is consistent with page faults on first touch of its fresh whole-file output allocation (64 MiB is about 16k faults on a VM). This is mibz2's minflt lever again: owned, reused output buffers matter.
- **rapidgzip -P4 barely scales** here. 10 MB of compressed Wikidata is only a few of its chunks, the VM is shared, and P1 is about 1.4× slower than igzip. Its parallel numbers need a corpus of gigabytes, not 64 MiB.

### 5\. Across cores (in memory, 1 MiB members dealt round-robin to threads)

|  | t1 | t2 | t3 | t4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| wikidata GB/s | 1.158 | 2.103 | **3.231** | 2.746 |
| binary GB/s | 0.593 | 1.123 | 1.502 | 1.633 |

Three threads scale nearly linearly. t4 on a shared 4-vCPU VM contends with everything else, so it says nothing about the i9.

## What has legs, and what to do next

1. **Drop single-thread interleaving as a lever.** Not worth carrying on real data. Revisit only for a kernel or data that is symbol-dense, such as huffman-only or literal-heavy blocks, and even then libdeflate's literal tricks get more.
2. **The single-thread kernel should match libdeflate.** Its techniques: decoding several literals per refill, `bitsleft -= entry` with pre-shifted entries, preloading the next entry before the current copy finishes, and 16- or 32-byte copies with an overrun budget. Its time is the per-worker cost of everything parallel, so it is the denominator of the whole speedrun. The open single-thread question is igzip against libdeflate in memory on the i9: igzip wins the single-member CLI runs here.
3. **The parallelism that pays is across cores, and the target is single-member** (the Wikidata dump is one 157 GB member). So the next experiment is the speculative chunk decode the brief made conditional, now conditioned on cores rather than ILP:
4. the cost of finding block starts on real data;
5. how fast unresolved-window markers thin out along a chunk (if they vanish within hundreds of KiB, the 16-bit marker pass is short and the rest runs at full speed);
6. the cost of the marker-resolution pass.

Measure it against rapidgzip on a multi-GB slice of the dump, not 64 MiB.

1. **Memory traffic is visible already:** first-touch faults on large output buffers cost libdeflate-gunzip about 40% of its CLI throughput here. Reuse owned buffers, size the ring of ready bytes, and fuse CRC into the copy or resolve pass.
2. **On the i9, with counters:** re-run `ours-k1` / `ours-k2` / `ours-k4` with `branch-misses`, `cycles` and port-utilisation counters. That would confirm or overturn the mispredict and port-pressure explanation, which is inferred here.

## Reproduce

```text
cargo build --release
python3 -I scripts/members.py corpus/{wikidata.json,source.tar,binary.tar}   # m1M + BGZF + .idx
python3 -I scripts/members_strategy.py corpus/wikidata.json huff corpus/wikidata.json.huff.gz
taskset -c 2 target/release/inflate-ilp corpus/wikidata.json.m1M.gz corpus/wikidata.json 12 \
    ours-k1,ours-k1-aa,ours-k2,ours-k4,ours-k4-r,libdeflate,zlib-ng > runs/x.txt
python3 scripts/ratio.py runs/x.txt ours-k1
cargo build --release --features census --target-dir target/census   # the symbol census
```

Raw rounds are in `runs/`. Corpus provenance: Wikidata is the first 64 MiB (whole lines) of `latest-all.json.gz` as served on 2026-11-22. Source and binary are tars of this container's Python stdlib, `/usr/include`, `/usr/bin` and `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`, each cut at 64 MiB.

# The single-thread kernel and the first parallel win (2026-11-22, session 2)

Same host as the first entry: a shared 4-vCPU VM (Sapphire Rapids-class Xeon at 2.1 GHz, 4 real cores, no hardware PMU). The build targets `x86-64-v3` (AVX2 + BMI2, the i9's ISA, no AVX-512). All ratios are paired, shuffled-order rounds with 95% t intervals on the log scale. Every arm is checked byte-exact against the reference before timing.

## Headline

On the 1.34 GB single-member Wikidata file (the real dump's head, recompressed with `gzip -6`), measured end to end (page-cache read, decode, CRC-32 and ISIZE checked, bytes to /dev/null):

|  | GB/s | time vs rapidgzip -P4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **upigz -P4, 1 MiB chunks (unchecked build)** | **1.21** | **0.677 \[0.616, 0.744\]** |
| **upigz -P4, 1 MiB chunks (safe build)** | **1.15** | **0.750 \[0.698, 0.807\]** (separate race) |
| upigz -P3 | 0.94 | 0.864 \[0.810, 0.921\] |
| rapidgzip 0.16.2 -P4 (default / `--verify`) | 0.80 / 0.82 | 1.000 / 0.980 |
| igzip (ISA-L 2.31), 1 thread | 0.81 | 1.003 |

So upigz runs at **1.33–1.48× rapidgzip's throughput on the same 4 cores**, and at P3 it already beats rapidgzip at P4. This is one host with 4 cores. rapidgzip scales poorly here (P2 is slower than its sequential P1 path), so the i9's 10 cores and 20 threads decide the real ranking.

Single thread, in memory (time vs libdeflate 1.26.1; GB/s for libdeflate):

|  | Wikidata -6 | source -6 | binary -6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| libdeflate | 1.106 GB/s | 0.657 | 0.546 |
| upigz kernel (unchecked) | 1.123 \[1.066, 1.183\] | 1.093 \[1.065, 1.122\] | 1.043 \[0.979, 1.112\] |
| upigz kernel (safe) | about 1.19–1.23 |  |  |
| ISA-L 2.31 | 1.172 | 1.138 | 1.149 |
| zlib-rs 0.6.8 | 1.366 | 1.410 | 1.391 |

Single-thread, upigz is second: ahead of ISA-L, zlib-rs and zlib-ng, behind libdeflate by 4–12% (unchecked) or about 20% (safe).

## The kernel (`src/fast.rs`): what moved it, step by step

Ratios are unchecked-build time vs libdeflate, on Wikidata / source / binary.

| step | ratios |
| --- | --- |
| v1: entry-driven consume, preload, 3 literals per refill, margins, word copies | 1.28 / 1.17 / 1.23 |
| unconditional first copy chunk (two 16-byte chunks, then libdeflate's 5×8) | no change |
| `bzhi`/`shrx` field extraction without masks, subtract the whole entry | no change |
| **libdeflate's literal→match fallthrough** (no refill on the transition) | **1.21 / 1.13 / 1.15** |
| **table build: libdeflate's doubling method for complete codes** | **1.07 / 1.09 / 1.09** |
| generic (inlined) entry constructors, 4 precode symbols per refill | 1.06 / 1.08 / 1.14 (noisy run) |

The safety tax (bounds checks the fast loop's margins make redundant) was 4–8% at v1, and is about 10–15% now that the rest is faster.

Profiling without a PMU: timing the block headers showed **dynamic headers plus table builds were 9–15% of decode time** at v1. Blocks average only 30–60 KB of output, so per-block fixed costs matter. That is now down to 3.5–6.5%.

## Parallel (`src/par.rs`)

### What the marker data showed first (`markers` mode)

These are speculative runs from real block starts with an unknown window. Each was checked symbol by symbol: literals equal the reference, and every marker resolves to the right byte.

- **Wikidata: markers never die.** The last marker lands at the end of the 16 MiB span in every sample, and 7–48% of output symbols are markers. Source and binary die out: median 1.6 and 4.4 MiB, p90 8.5 and 10.2 MiB.
- **Markers are fragmented**: runs average about 2 symbols, and 24–60% of Wikidata matches copy at least one marker. Only 1–6K distinct window bytes are ever referenced.
- So "switch to bytes once markers die" fails on the target, and so does an out-of-band marker-run table. On Wikidata a 16-bit pass over the whole chunk is unavoidable.

### The pipeline

1. **Finder.** A parallel bit-by-bit scan per chunk. The prefilter checks BFINAL=0, BTYPE=2, HLIT and HDIST in range, and a complete precode. Then a strict header parse requires complete litlen and distance codes and an end-of-block code. It costs 9–23 ms for 186 chunks on 195 MB of input.
2. **Pass 1.** Chunk 0 decodes straight to bytes. Chunk k≥1 decodes to `u16` from 32 768 window markers, with the same generic kernel as the byte path (`Sym` trait), until a block starts at or past the next chunk's start. It must land on that start exactly, which checks the finder.
3. **Windows.** Each chunk's last 32 KiB is resolved through the previous chunk's window, in order.
4. **Resolve and CRC** in parallel. Per-chunk CRC-32s are combined in order (`crc32fast::Hasher::combine`); the CRC and ISIZE are checked against the trailer.

### Getting from 0.55 to 1.21 GB/s end to end: the same lessons as mibz2

| version | upigz -P4 time vs rapidgzip -P4 |
| --- | --- |
| all chunks alive at once, decode then CRC then write run in sequence (1.69 GB/s in memory, warm buffers) | 1.591 \[1.194, 2.119\] |
| **bounded**: at most threads+2 chunks in flight, recycled buffers, streamed output | 0.849 \[0.793, 0.909\] |
| resolution as a queued task (a regression: it exposed a serial chain) | 1.130 \[1.029, 1.241\] |
| **window hand-off taken off the resolution chain** (next window derived before a chunk is queued; separate cursors for windows and writes) | **0.677 \[0.616, 0.744\]** |

The first version lost because of about a million first-touch page faults (around 2.7 GB of 16-bit buffers plus 1.34 GB of bytes) and phases that ran one after another. The in-memory harness hid this because it reuses warm buffers.

The third row is a who-waits-on-whom bug. The window for chunk k+1 came from chunk k's symbols, but a worker could already have taken those symbols to resolve chunk k. That made every resolution wait for the previous one.

## Open, in order

1. **The re-decode bet** (the candidate key idea; see the session chat). Pass 1 into a cache-resident 16-bit ring that keeps only the final window, then a real byte decode per chunk from its known window. That costs two decodes of compute but about 1.6 B/B of DRAM traffic, against roughly 5 B/B for the current marker-resolve design.
2. Measure first: pass 1 alone, against a byte decode.
3. The decisive test is a thread sweep on the i9, where the marker-resolve design should go memory-bound.
4. **The 16-bit pass-1 kernel is slow.** One-thread `par` is 0.47 GB/s, against 1.03 for the byte kernel.
5. **Robustness the prototype doesn't have:**
6. finder false positives (they error out; they don't recover);
7. chunks shorter than a window;
8. multi-member files and the dump's 2-byte leading member;
9. corrupt-input error parity with zlib;
10. fuzzing.
11. **Closing libdeflate single-thread:**
12. the remaining table-build cost;
13. multi-literal entries (ISA-L-style packed literals);
14. removing the safe-build tax without `unsafe` (restructuring so that LLVM can prove the bounds).
15. **On the i9:** the full thread sweep (1–20), DRAM bytes per output byte, peak RSS and minflt for upigz and rapidgzip. Then register the re-decode verdict rule before running.

# Speculative decode: the theorem, checked before any proof (2026-11-22)

Sources:

- the lean-zip inventory (`kim-em/lean-zip` @ 2f7a63f3, read only);
- `spectest` in `src/main.rs`, a programmatic counterexample hunt.

## Setting

Let `S` be a valid raw DEFLATE stream (as bits). Sequential inflate produces `out`, and visits blocks `B_0 … B_m`; block `B_j` starts at bit `p_j` with output offset `o_j`. The decoder reads blocks one after another, so `p_j` are exactly the bit positions at which the sequential decoder reads a block header. A position that merely parses as a header is not one of them.

The symbolic window is `M = (μ_0 … μ_32767)`, where `μ_w` stands for the byte `32768 − w` before the chunk start. `D(p, M)` is speculative decode from bit `p` over the alphabet `bytes ∪ M`: copies move symbols, so markers propagate through overlapping copies too. `resolve(Y, W)` replaces each `μ_w` in `Y` with `W[w]`.

## (a) Composition and resolution, given a valid boundary

For every block start `p_j`, and every later block start `p_q` (or the end of the stream):

1. **Same path.** `D(p_j, M)` decodes successfully, and reads exactly the same block headers and the same bits as the sequential decoder, stopping at `p_q`. This holds because symbol decoding (headers, Huffman tables, codes) never reads the history. In lean-zip only `resolveLZ77` touches `acc`; `decodeSymbols` and `decodeDynamicTables` never do.
2. **Length.** `|D(p_j, M)| = o_q − o_j`.
3. **Resolution.** `resolve(D(p_j, M), W_j) = out[o_j .. o_q)`, where `W_j = out[o_j − 32768 .. o_j)`.
4. **Absent history is never referenced.** If `o_j < 32768`, no `μ_w` with `w < 32768 − o_j` occurs in `D(p_j, M)`. That follows from `S` being valid: the sequential decoder would have rejected such a distance. For an *invalid* `S` this is exactly where speculative and sequential decoding can disagree, so the statement needs `S` valid, or a side condition.
5. **Window chaining.** `W_q = resolve(last 32 KiB of D(p_j, M), W_j)`, when `o_q − o_j ≥ 32768`. This is the serial hand-off: 32 KiB of work per chunk.

## (b) Finding boundaries

Here a chunk-start candidate `s` comes from a heuristic finder.

**Chaining lemma.** Let `p` be a true block start. Suppose `D(p, ·)` reaches a block start at exactly bit `s` (the first block start `≥ s` *equals* `s`). Then `s` is a true block start. The reason is that decoding is deterministic and (a)1 says `D` follows the sequential path.

**Corollary (pipeline soundness).** Chunk 0 starts at the stream start, which is a true boundary. By induction over chunks, every candidate accepted by the equality check is true. A false positive is never used; it can only cost time, by falling back to merging chunks. **The finder therefore needs no proof for correctness, only for performance.** Its heuristics (precode completeness, code completeness) bound wasted work, not the result.

## Evidence before proof

`spectest 6000` builds random streams with miniz\_oxide at levels 0–10, so stored, fixed and dynamic blocks all occur. The data is random, text-like, run-heavy and overlap-heavy (periodic patterns with period 1–12, repeats up to 40 KiB back).

At **every** block start (16,046 of them, 7,556 with history shorter than 32 KiB) it checks (a)1–4 on both the reference-style `spec.rs` decoder and the production `u16` kernel in `fast.rs`. It found **no counterexample**. Earlier, the `markers` mode had checked (a)3 symbol by symbol on 48 real-corpus chunks of 16 MiB.

## The proof opportunity in lean-zip (estimate from the inventory: medium, about 500–1,500 lines)

What it reuses:

- **The spec, and two-way equivalence to the native decoder.** `inflateLoop_correct` / `inflateLoop_complete` hold from any bit position with any prior output, and `inflate_ok_iff_decodesTo` covers arbitrary streams.
- **Lemmas about history and suffixes:** `resolveLZ77_shift`, `resolveLZ77_append_eobFree`, `decode_go_suffix` and `decode_go_acc_prefix`.

What has to be new:

- a version of `resolveLZ77` and `decode.go` that works over any symbol alphabet;
- a lemma that resolution commutes with substituting the true window;
- a decoder-side `dist ≤ 32768` bound;
- a both-directions lemma that the full history is equivalent to its last 32 KiB;
- a decoder that stops at a given block;
- (a)5 and the chaining lemma.

Obstacles:

- everything is hard-wired to `UInt8`, so the generic alphabet should be a copy, not a refactor;
- `alignToByte` works from the number of bits remaining, so a chunk must be a suffix of the stream's bits plus a stop point;
- the `maxOutputSize` bookkeeping counts the earlier history.

## Engineering value

1. **Safety checks can be narrower.** With the chaining lemma, correctness never depends on the finder. rapidgzip-style validation (decoding far to confirm a candidate) is purely a performance choice.
2. **The re-decode design needs less new proof than marker resolution.** Its pass 2 is ordinary inflate from a block boundary with a known history. lean-zip already has that (`inflateLoop_correct`), given the 32 KiB-suffix lemma. Pass 1 needs (a) only for the final window.
3. **What it can't do:** prove that the Rust code is correct. That link stays differential testing (`spectest`, the byte-exact harness) and fuzzing. And it says nothing about speed.

## Decision

The statement holds under testing and is precise enough to formalise. It isn't on the performance critical path, so I'd **start it as a separate, bounded line** of about 500–1,500 lines of Lean, scoped to (a) plus the chaining lemma. It should run on its own `research/` branch once the repo exists, and shouldn't hold up benchmark work.

# One gzip member, four cores: decoding Wikidata 1.48× faster than rapidgzip

On a 4-core research VM, upigz decodes a 1.34 GB single-member Wikidata gzip in 0.68× rapidgzip's time, CRC checked, and its one-thread kernel is within 4–12% of libdeflate.

22 November 2026 · 6 min read · [Research in progress](<#what-isnt-known-yet>)

upigz is a gzip decoder in Rust, built for one hard case: a single huge gzip member, like the 157 GB Wikidata JSON dump. These are its first measurements, all taken on a shared 4-vCPU cloud VM rather than the 10-core workstation that will decide the real ranking.

- **Parallel:** decoding a 1.34 GB single-member Wikidata file end to end, CRC-32 and size checked, upigz on 4 threads takes **0.677× the time of rapidgzip on 4 threads** (95% CI \[0.616, 0.744\]): **1.21 GB/s against 0.80**. The build with no `unsafe` code takes 0.750× \[0.698, 0.807\].
- **One thread:** upigz's kernel takes **1.04–1.12× libdeflate's time** on Wikidata, source code and binaries. That's second place: ahead of ISA-L and zlib-rs, not yet level with libdeflate.
- **Not yet known:** how either result holds on the 10-core, 20-thread i9 workstation. No run there has been registered yet.

Below: [why one member is the hard case](<#why-one-member-is-the-hard-case>), [the parallel result](<#the-parallel-result>), [the one-thread kernel](<#the-one-thread-kernel>), [what didn't work](<#what-didnt-work>) and [what isn't known yet](<#what-isnt-known-yet>).

## Why one member is the hard case

A gzip file made of many small members, as BGZF files in bioinformatics are, is easy to decode in parallel: each member is independent. The Wikidata dump isn't like that. Its head is a 22-byte member holding `[` and a newline, followed by one member of 157 GB.

Inside one member, DEFLATE gives nothing for free. Blocks start at arbitrary bit positions with no marker, and a match may copy from anywhere in the previous 32 KiB of output, including output of earlier blocks. A worker that starts decoding in the middle doesn't know that history.

upigz does what rapidgzip does:

1. It finds a block start near each chunk boundary.
2. It decodes from there with 32,768 placeholders, *markers*, standing for the unknown history.
3. It hands each chunk's final 32 KiB to the next chunk in order, and replaces the markers with real bytes.

Each chunk must stop exactly where the next one starts. That check makes a false block match harmless: a candidate is used only if the previous chunk's real decode lands on it.

## The parallel result

End to end on the 1.34 GB single-member Wikidata file (`gzip -6`): read from the page cache, decode, check CRC-32 and size, write to /dev/null. Six paired rounds in shuffled order (`runs/race-big4.txt`). The time ratio is the geometric mean of per-round ratios, with a 95% interval. rapidgzip 0.16.2's default and `--verify` forms ran at the same speed (0.980 \[0.884, 1.085\]).

On four threads upigz runs at 1.48× rapidgzip's throughput. On three threads it already beats rapidgzip on four: 0.864× the time \[0.810, 0.921\]. Removing all `unsafe` code from the decoder costs a little: in a separate race the safe build took 0.750× rapidgzip's time \[0.698, 0.807\], against 0.722 for the unchecked build in the same race.

The decoding itself wasn't what made the difference. Two memory and scheduling fixes were:

- **Bounded memory.** The first version kept every chunk alive at once: about 2.7 GB of 16-bit symbols plus 1.34 GB of bytes, first touched in a fresh process. It took 1.59× rapidgzip's time. Capping the chunks in flight at the thread count plus two, recycling their buffers and streaming the output brought that to 0.849×.
- **A serial chain removed.** Each chunk's window came from the previous chunk's symbols, but a worker could take those symbols to resolve that chunk first, so every resolution waited for the one before. Deriving the next window before queuing a chunk brought the time to 0.677×.

## The one-thread kernel

One thread, in memory, decoding 64 MiB inputs at `gzip -6` into a reused buffer, no CRC. Eleven paired rounds per corpus (`runs/sota-*.txt`). The dashed line is libdeflate; whiskers are 95% intervals. libdeflate's own A/A control landed at 0.987–1.006.

upigz's kernel follows libdeflate's design: each table entry says how many bits to consume, the next entry is looked up before the current match is copied, and up to three literals decode on one refill of the bit buffer. Two steps closed most of the gap:

- **Falling from literals straight into a match**, without refilling the bit buffer, as libdeflate does.
- **Building each block's decode tables libdeflate's way**, filling the shortest codes first and doubling. Block headers and table builds had cost 9–15% of the whole decode, because the blocks are small (30–60 KB of output each).

It is now second: it takes 1.123× libdeflate's time on Wikidata, 1.093× on source code and 1.043× on binaries \[0.979, 1.112\]. ISA-L takes 1.14–1.17× and zlib-rs 1.37–1.41×. These figures are from the research build with unchecked memory access; with bounds checks the kernel is about 1.2× libdeflate's time.

## What didn't work

- **Interleaving within one thread.** mibz2, upigz's bzip2 sibling, gained a lot by walking several independent chains in one thread. For gzip, decoding 2–8 independent members round-robin was never faster than one after another on real data: 0.98–1.13× the time. The idea does work on streams of literals only (about 1.28× faster), but real gzip data is mostly matches: 0.12–0.25 symbols per output byte, with 84–92% of bytes coming from matches.
- **Waiting for the markers to die.** If the unknown history stopped being referenced after a few hundred KiB, a worker could switch to plain bytes and skip most of the 16-bit pass. On source code and binaries markers do die out (median 1.6 and 4.4 MiB). On Wikidata JSON they never do: 7–48% of all output symbols were still markers across 16 MiB spans, because the same keys and structure keep being copied forward.

## What isn't known yet

- **Every number here is from a shared 4-vCPU cloud VM** with no hardware counters. On that host rapidgzip scales oddly: in one run it decoded at 0.74 GB/s on one thread but 0.48 on two. The i9-10900K workstation decides, through recipes whose decision rules are written down before the data. None has been registered or run yet.
- **The parallel decoder is a prototype.** If the block finder matches a false block, it stops with an error instead of recovering. It doesn't handle chunks shorter than 32 KiB, multi-member files or corrupt input yet, and hasn't been fuzzed.
- **Correctness so far** is byte-exact output and the CRC check on every timed run. It is also a counterexample hunt: 16,046 restarts from block boundaries in 6,000 random streams, with no mismatch ([the theorem](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/speculative-theorem/index.md>)).

Next, the bet that upigz is built around: instead of storing 16-bit symbols for the whole chunk and resolving them later, decode each chunk twice. The first pass keeps only its final window, in cache; the second is an ordinary byte decode from the known history, straight into the output. That spends twice the decoding work to move, by our estimate, about a third as much data through memory: roughly 1.6 bytes per output byte instead of 5. The thread sweep on the i9 will show whether that trade pays.

The evidence is in the journals: [interleaving](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/interleaved-inflate/index.md>), [the kernel and the first parallel win](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/kernel-and-parallel/index.md>) and [the speculative-decode theorem](<https://lmmx.github.io/upigz/journal/speculative-theorem/index.md>).
